questions.question: In figure, the capacitor initially has a charge of \(10\text{ Coulomb}\). The current in the circuit one second after the switch S is closed will be
questions.explanation: Given, \[Q(0^-)=10~\text{C}, \qquad C=0.5~\text{F}\] Therefore, the initial capacitor voltage is \[V_C(0^-) = \frac{Q(0^-)}{C} = \frac{10}{0.5} = 20~\text{V}\] Since the voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously, \[V_C(0^+) = V_C(0^-) = 20~\text{V}\] At steady state \((t\to\infty)\), the capacitor behaves as an open circuit. \[V_C(\infty) = 100~\text{V}\] For an RC charging circuit, \[V_C(t) = V_C(\infty) + \left[ V_C(0^+)-V_C(\infty) \right] e^{-t/RC}\] Substituting, \[R=2~\Omega, \qquad C=0.5~\text{F}\] \[RC = 2\times0.5 = 1~\text{s}\] Therefore, \[V_C(t) = 100+(20-100)e^{-t}\] \[V_C(t) = 100-80e^{-t}\] The capacitor current is \[i_C(t) = C\frac{dV_C(t)}{dt}= 0.5\frac{d}{dt} \left( 100-80e^{-t} \right)\] \[i_C(t) = 0.5 \left( 80e^{-t} \right)= 40e^{-t}\ \text{A}\] At \(t=1~\text{s}\), \[i_C(1) = 40e^{-1}\] \[i_C(1) \approx 14.71~\text{A}\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }14.7~\text{A}}\]

The total admittance \(Z\) of the network is given by: \[Z = R+ \frac{1}{j\omega C} || j\omega L\] The admittance of the parallel part is : \[Y=\frac{1}{j\omega L} + j\omega C\] For the imaginary part of the admittance to equal zero: \[\omega C - \frac{1}{\omega L} = 0\] Solving for capacitance \(C\): \[C = \frac{1}{\omega^2 L}\] Given parameters from the circuit problem: Frequency, \(f = 500\,\text{Hz}\) Inductance, \(L = 2\,\text{H}\) Angular frequency, \(\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 500\,\text{rad/s}\) Substituting these values into the capacitance equation: \[C = \frac{1}{(2\pi \times 500)^2 \times 2}\] \[C = 5.066 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{F}\] \[C = 0.05\,\mu\text{F}\] \[\boxed{(d)0.05\,\mu\text{F}}\]

questions.question: Total instantaneous power supplied by a 3-phase ac supply to a balanced R-L load is
questions.explanation:
To find the total instantaneous power supplied by a balanced 3-phase AC supply to a balanced R-L load, we derive the sum of the instantaneous power of all three phases. Let the balanced three-phase source voltages be represented as: \[v_A(t) = V_m \sin(\omega t)\] \[v_B(t) = V_m \sin(\omega t - 120^\circ)\] \[v_C(t) = V_m \sin(\omega t - 240^\circ)\] Since the load is a balanced R-L load, the currents will lag the corresponding phase voltages by an impedance phase angle \(\phi\): \[i_A(t) = I_m \sin(\omega t - \phi)\] \[i_B(t) = I_m \sin(\omega t - 120^\circ - \phi)\] \[i_C(t) = I_m \sin(\omega t - 240^\circ - \phi)\] The total instantaneous power \(p(t)\) is the sum of the individual phase powers: \[p(t) = v_A(t)i_A(t) + v_B(t)i_B(t) + v_C(t)i_C(t)\] Applying the trigonometric identity \(\sin(X)\sin(Y) = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(X-Y) - \cos(X+Y)]\) to each phase: For Phase A: \[v_A(t)i_A(t) = \frac{V_m I_m}{2} \left[ \cos(\phi) - \cos(2\omega t - \phi) \right]\] For Phase B: \[v_B(t)i_B(t) = \frac{V_m I_m}{2} \left[ \cos(\phi) - \cos(2\omega t - 240^\circ - \phi) \right]\] For Phase C: \[v_C(t)i_C(t) = \frac{V_m I_m}{2} \left[ \cos(\phi) - \cos(2\omega t - 480^\circ - \phi) \right]\] Summing these three equations together: \[p(t) = \frac{V_m I_m}{2} [3\cos(\phi)] - \frac{V_m I_m}{2} \left[ \cos(2\omega t - \phi) + \cos(2\omega t - 240^\circ - \phi) + \cos(2\omega t - 480^\circ - \phi) \right]\] The three double-frequency cosine terms inside the brackets represent a balanced three-phase set of sinusoidal quantities separated by \(120^\circ\) (\(480^\circ\) is co-terminal with \(120^\circ\)). The sum of any balanced three-phase sinusoidal set at any instant is identically zero: \[\cos(2\omega t - \phi) + \cos(2\omega t - 120^\circ - \phi) + \cos(2\omega t - 240^\circ - \phi) = 0\] Therefore, the time-dependent pulsating components completely cancel out, leaving: \[p(t) = \frac{3}{2} V_m I_m \cos(\phi) = 3 V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos(\phi)\] Since \(V_{rms}\), \(I_{rms}\), and \(\cos(\phi)\) are time-invariant constants for a steady balanced system, the total instantaneous power remains absolutely constant with respect to time. \[\boxed{(b)\textit{Constant}}\]
Key points
  • The total constant instantaneous power of a balanced three-phase system equals three times the average active power per phase.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse single-phase power traits with three-phase power traits; while single-phase real power is pulsating, balanced three-phase real power is invariant.

options: both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are reverse biased.
the base-emitter junctions is reverse biased, and the base-collector junction is forward biased.
the base-emitter junction is forward biased, and the base-collector junction is reverse biased.
both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are forward biased.
questions.explanation:
When a BJT is in the saturation region, both the base-emitter and collector-base junctions are forward biased. \[\boxed{\text{D) Saturation}}\]
Key points
  • Active Region: Emitter-base junction forward biased, collector-base junction reverse biased (acts as an amplifier).
  • Saturation Region: Emitter-base junction forward biased, collector-base junction forward biased (acts as an ON switch).
  • Cut-off Region: Both junctions reverse biased (acts as an OFF switch).
  • Inverse Active Region: Emitter-base junction reverse biased, collector-base junction forward biased.

questions.question: A digital circuit which compares two numbers \(A_3\,A_2\,A_1\,A_0\), \(B_3\,B_2\,B_1\,B_0\) is shown in the figure. To get output \(Y = 0\), choose one pair of correct input numbers.
questions.explanation:
Given: A digital comparator circuit using XOR gates for 4-bit numbers \(A_3A_2A_1A_0\) and \(B_3B_2B_1B_0\). Output \(Y = 0\) is required. From the circuit, each XOR gate compares corresponding bits: \[Y_i = A_i \oplus B_i\] The final output is the NAND of all XOR outputs: \[Y = \overline{Y_3 \cdot Y_2 \cdot Y_1 \cdot Y_0}\] For \(Y = 0\), the NAND output must be 0, which requires all inputs to the NAND to be 1: \[Y_3 = Y_2 = Y_1 = Y_0 = 1 \implies A_i \neq B_i \text{ for all } i\] Checking option (D): \(A = 1010\), \(B = 0101\): \[A_3 \oplus B_3 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1, \quad A_2 \oplus B_2 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1, \quad A_1 \oplus B_1 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1, \quad A_0 \oplus B_0 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1\] \[Y = \overline{1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1} = \overline{1} = 0 \quad \checkmark\] Options (A), (B), (C) have \(A = B\), so all XOR outputs are 0, giving \(Y = \overline{0} = 1 \neq 0\). \[\boxed{A = 1010,\; B = 0101}\]
Key points
  • An XOR gate acts as a 1-bit inequality detector: output is 1 when inputs differ.
  • A NAND gate following the XOR chain produces 0 only when all bits differ between \(A\) and \(B\).
Hence, the correct option is (D). (D) 1010,;0101.

questions.question: The digital circuit shown in figure generates a modified clock pulse at the output. Choose the correct output waveform from the options given below.
questions.explanation:
Given \(J\)-\(K\) flip-flop is shown below,
1. Functional Logic Derivation:
We analyze the behavior of the sequential circuit step-by-step:
  • Steering Inputs: The inputs are tied to a permanent high logic level (\(J = 1\) and \(K = 1\)). This configures the \(J\)-\(K\) flip-flop to operate permanently in toggle mode.
  • Clock Triggering: The clock terminal features an inversion bubble, meaning the flip-flop is negative-edge triggered. Consequently, the output \(Q\) will change state only at the falling edge (\(\downarrow\)) of the \(\text{CLK}\) signal.
  • Output Expression: The combinational logic stage at the output features a 2-input AND gate whose inputs are driven directly by the true output \(Q\) of the flip-flop and the external clock signal (\(\text{CLK}\)). Thus, the explicit output expression is: \[\text{O/P} = Q \cdot \text{CLK}\]
From this expression, it is clear that the final network output (\(\text{O/P}\)) can be high (\(\text{logic } 1\)) if and only if both \(Q\) and \(\text{CLK}\) are simultaneously high. 2. Initial State and Waveform Analysis:
Because no initial state information is specified for the flip-flop output \(Q\), we can arbitrarily choose an initial condition to trace the timing sequence. Let us assume the initial state is reset (\(Q = 0\)). Note that choosing the alternative state (\(Q = 1\)) merely shifts the starting phase, but the ultimate periodic, steady-state characteristics of the output waveform remain identical. With \(Q = 0\) initially:
  • During the first clock cycle, \(Q = 0\). Since \(\text{O/P} = 0 \cdot \text{CLK} = 0\), the overall circuit output stays low.
  • At the first negative edge (\(\downarrow\)) of \(\text{CLK}\), the flip-flop toggles, making \(Q = 1\).
  • During this second clock cycle, \(Q\) remains high. Therefore, when \(\text{CLK}\) goes high, the output follows: \(\text{O/P} = 1 \cdot 1 = 1\). When \(\text{CLK}\) drops low, \(\text{O/P} = 1 \cdot 0 = 0\).
  • This process alternates continuously, resulting in the output pulse being generated only during the intervals where the high phases of \(\text{CLK}\) and \(Q\) overlap.
Hence, the correct option is (B). (B) [Waveform: AND output high only during overlap of CLK high and Q high]
Key points
  • When \(J=K=1\), the flip-flop halves the frequency of the input clock at its \(Q\) output terminal.
  • Gating the output \(Q\) with the original \(\text{CLK}\) through an AND gate clips the pulse duration, matching the exact overlapping interval when both signals are high.

questions.question: The voltage comparator shown in figure can be used in the analog-to-digital conversion as
questions.explanation:
A voltage comparator has two inputs \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) and one output \(V_0\): Case I: When \(V_1 < V_2\), the output voltage \(V_0\) is \(+V_{set}\), i.e., High (logic-1). Case II: When \(V_1 > V_2\), the output voltage \(V_0\) is \(-V_{set}\), i.e., Low (logic-0). \(V_0\) can assume only one of two possible values: High or Low, corresponding to logic-1 and logic-0. This represents a 1-bit digital output. Therefore, a voltage comparator can be used as a 1-bit quantizer in analog-to-digital conversion. (A) A 1-bit quantizer
Key points
  • A single comparator produces a 1-bit output (two levels: high or low).
  • A flash ADC uses \(2^n - 1\) comparators to produce an \(n\)-bit digital output simultaneously.
  • For an 8-bit flash ADC, \(2^8 - 1 = 255\) comparators are required.

questions.question: For a tachometer if \(\theta(t)\) is the rotor displacement is radians, \(e(t)\) is the output voltage and \(K_t\) is the tachometer constant in V/rad/sec, then the transfer function, \(\dfrac{E(s)}{\Theta(s)}\) will be
questions.explanation:
A tachometer (or DC tachogenerator) is an electromechanical device that converts mechanical angular velocity into an electrical voltage signal. The output voltage \(e(t)\) generated by a tachometer is directly proportional to its angular speed \(\omega(t)\): \[e(t) = K_t \omega(t)\] where \(\omega(t)\) is the derivative of the rotor displacement \(\theta(t)\) with respect to time: \(\omega(t) = \dfrac{d\theta(t)}{dt}\) \[e(t) = K_t \frac{d\theta(t)}{dt}\] Taking the Laplace transform on both sides under zero initial conditions: \(E(s) = K_t \cdot s\Theta(s)\) \[\frac{E(s)}{\Theta(s)} = K_t s\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ K_t s}\]
Key points
  • When the input is rotor displacement \(\theta(t)\), the transfer function is given by: \(\dfrac{E(s)}{\Theta(s)} = K_t s\)
  • When the input is angular velocity \(\omega(t)\), the transfer function is given by: \(\dfrac{E(s)}{\Omega(s)} = K_t\)

questions.explanation: The unit impulse response of the system is given by: \(c(t) = 12.5e^{-6t} \sin 8t \cdot u(t)\) The transfer function \(G(s)\) of a system is equal to the Laplace transform of its unit impulse response under zero initial conditions. Using the standard Laplace transform pairs and property \(\mathcal{L}\{e^{-at}\sin\omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{(s+a)^2 + \omega^2}\): \[G(s) = 12.5 \times \frac{8}{(s+6)^2 + 8^2} = \frac{100}{s^2 + 12s + 100}\] For a unit step input, \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\), the output response in the \(s\)-domain is: \[C(s) = R(s) \cdot G(s) = \frac{1}{s} \cdot \frac{100}{s^2 + 12s + 100}\] Using the Final Value Theorem, the steady-state value of the response is: \[C_{\text{ss}} = \lim_{s \to 0} sC(s) =\lim_{s \to 0} s \left[ \frac{1}{s} \cdot \frac{100}{s^2 + 12s + 100} \right] = \frac{100}{0 + 0 + 100} = 1\] \[\boxed{(D) \ \ 1}\]

The following motor definitely has a permanent magnet rotor
questions.explanation:
A permanent magnet stepper motor has a rotor made of ferrite or rare-earth material that is permanently magnetized. The motor rotates through a fixed angle, called the step angle, for each electrical pulse received by its control unit. Since the rotor position is directly related to the number of input pulses, position and speed control can be achieved without feedback sensors. \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points

  • Each input pulse produces a discrete angular displacement called a step.
  • Stepper motors convert digital pulse inputs into mechanical motion.
  • Open-loop operation eliminates the need for position or speed sensors in many applications.

  • The rotor rotates in the same direction as the rotating magnetic field.

questions.question: For a \(1.8^\circ\), 2-phase bipolar stepper motor, the stepping rate is \(100\) steps/second. The rotational speed of the motor in rpm is
questions.explanation:
For a stepper motor, the speed is given by \[N=\frac{\beta f}{360}\] where
  • \(\beta\) = step angle in degrees
  • \(f\) = stepping rate in steps/second
Given, \[\beta=1.8^\circ\] \[f=100\,\text{steps/s}\] Substituting, \[N=\frac{1.8\times100}{360}\] \[N=0.5\,\text{rps}\] Converting into rpm, \[N=0.5\times60\] \[N=30\,\text{rpm}\] Hence, the rotational speed of the motor is \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • Stepper motor speed is directly proportional to both step angle and stepping frequency.
  • Speed in revolutions per second is given by \(N=\dfrac{\beta f}{360}\).
  • To convert rps into rpm, multiply by \(60\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget to convert rps into rpm by multiplying by \(60\).
  • Use step angle in degrees while applying the speed formula.
  • Do not confuse stepping rate (steps/s) with rotational speed (rpm).

questions.question: For a given stepper motor, the following torque has the highest numerical value.
questions.explanation:
For a stepper motor, the torque ratings satisfy \[T_{\text{pull-out}} > T_{\text{holding}} > T_{\text{pull-in}} > T_{\text{detent}}\] where
  • Detent torque is the torque present when the winding is unexcited.
  • Holding torque is the maximum static torque with the winding excited.
  • Pull-in torque is the maximum load torque at which the motor can start, stop, or reverse without losing steps.
  • Pull-out torque is the maximum torque that the motor can deliver while running synchronously.
Hence, the highest numerical value is the pull-out torque. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Pull-out torque is the maximum operating torque of a stepper motor.
  • Holding torque is measured under energized standstill conditions.
  • Detent torque exists even when the motor winding is not energized.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse holding torque with pull-out torque.
  • Detent torque is always smaller than holding torque.
  • Pull-in torque is not the maximum torque capability of the motor.

questions.explanation: Reluctance torque depends on the variation of inductance with rotor position. \[T_r=\frac{1}{2}i^2\frac{dL}{d\theta}\] If the inductance is independent of rotor position, then \[\frac{dL}{d\theta}=0\] Hence, reluctance is also not varying with rotor position. This means the machine has a cylindrical rotor structure with uniform reluctance and uniform air-gap. Therefore, reluctance torque should be zero. Reluctance torque is produced only when the rotor tends to align itself along the path of minimum reluctance. \[\boxed{ D}\]

questions.question: A moving-iron ammeter produces a full scale torque of \(240\,\mu\text{Nm}\) with a deflection of \(120^\circ\) at a current of \(10\,\text{A}\). The rate of change of self-inductance (\(\mu\text{H/radian}\)) of the instrument at full scale is
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[T_d=240\,\mu\text{Nm}=240\times10^{-6}\,\text{Nm},\qquad I=10\,\text{A}\] For a moving iron instrument, \[T_d=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta}\] Hence, \[\frac{dL}{d\theta}=\frac{2T_d}{I^2}\] Substituting, \[\frac{dL}{d\theta} = \frac{2(240\times10^{-6})}{10^2} = \frac{480\times10^{-6}}{100} = 4.8\times10^{-6}\,\text{H/rad}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }4.8\,\mu\text{H/radian}}\]

questions.question: A DC ampere hour meter is rated for \(15\,\text{A}\), \(250\,\text{V}\). The meter constant is \(14.4\,\text{A seconds/rev}\). The meter constant at rated voltage may be expressed as
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[V=250\,\text{V},\qquad I=15\,\text{A}\] Meter constant: \[14.4\,\text{A}\\\ \text{s/rev}\] This means charge per revolution is \[Q=14.4\,\text{A}\cdot\text{s}\] Energy consumed per revolution: \[E_{\text{rev}}=VQ=250\times14.4=3600\,\text{W}\cdot\text{s}\] Since \[1\,\text{Wh}=3600\,\text{W}\cdot\text{s}\] therefore, \[E_{\text{rev}}=1\,\text{Wh}\] Hence, \[1\,\text{rev}=1\,\text{Wh}\] Therefore, \[1000\,\text{rev}=1000\,\text{Wh}=1\,\text{kWh}\] So the meter constant is \[\boxed{1000\,\text{rev/kWh}}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }1000\,\text{rev/kWh}}\]

questions.explanation:
Given:
\[N=100,\qquad B=200\,\text{mT}=0.2\,\text{T}\] \[l=10\,\text{mm}=10\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\] \[d=20\,\text{mm}=20\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\] \[I=50\,\text{mA}=0.05\,\text{A}\] For a PMMC instrument, \[T=NBIA\] where coil area is \[A=l\times d\] Thus, \[A=(10\times10^{-3})(20\times10^{-3}) =2\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2\] Substituting, \[T=100\times0.2\times0.05\times2\times10^{-4}\] Hence, \[T=2\times10^{-4}\,\text{Nm}\] Converting into \(\mu\text{Nm}\), \[T=2\times10^{-4}\times10^6 =200\,\mu\text{Nm}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }200\,\mu\text{Nm}}\]

questions.question: A galvanometer with a full scale current of \(10\,\text{mA}\) has a resistance of \(1000\,\Omega\). The multiplying power (the ratio of measured current to galvanometer current) of a \(100\,\Omega\) shunt with this galvanometer is
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[I_g=10\,\text{mA}=0.01\,\text{A},\qquad R_g=1000\,\Omega,\qquad R_{sh}=100\,\Omega\] Since galvanometer and shunt are in parallel, \[I_gR_g=I_{sh}R_{sh}\] Substituting, \[0.01\times1000=I_{sh}\times100\] \[10=100I_{sh} \Rightarrow I_{sh}=0.1\,\text{A}\] Hence total measurable current is \[I=I_g+I_{sh}=0.01+0.1=0.11\,\text{A}\] Multiplying power: \[m=\frac{I}{I_g} = \frac{0.11}{0.01} =11\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }11}\]

questions.question: The circuit in the given figure is used to measure the power consumed by the load. The current coil and the voltage coil of the wattmeter have \(0.02\,\Omega\) and \(1000\,\Omega\) resistances, respectively. The measured power compared to the load power will be [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[R_{PC}=1000\,\Omega,\qquad R_{CC}=0.02\,\Omega,\qquad V_{\text{load}}=200\,\text{V},\qquad I_{\text{load}}=20\,\text{A}\] [figure unavailable] From the figure, the pressure coil is connected before the current coil, so the pressure coil voltage is \[V_1=V_{\text{load}}+I_{\text{load}}R_{CC}\] \[V_1=200+(20)(0.02)=200.4\,\text{V}\] Current through the pressure coil is \[I_{PC}=\frac{V_1}{R_{PC}}=\frac{200.4}{1000}=0.2004\,\text{A}\] Hence current through the current coil is \[I_1=I_{\text{load}}+I_{PC}=20+0.2004=20.2004\,\text{A}\] However, the wattmeter reading is \[P_m=V_1I_1\] Since pressure coil current contribution is negligible, error comes mainly from the current coil loss: \[P_m=V_{\text{load}}I_{\text{load}}+I_{\text{load}}^2R_{CC}\] \[P_m=(200)(20)+20^2(0.02)=4000+8=4008\,\text{W}\] True load power: \[P_{\text{load}}=200\times20=4000\,\text{W}\] Percentage error: \[\%\text{ error}=\frac{4008-4000}{4000}\times100=0.2\%\] Thus, the measured power is 0.2% more than the load power. Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }\text{0.2\% more}}\]
